items.excerpt: In 'Love Machine' (Faber & Faber), sociologist James Muldoon reports on people's intimate relationships with AI chatbots — he built his own companion 'Jasmine' to research it — and argues the bond is 'such a pale imitation' of human friendship, even as it sustains isolated readers.

BookTok creators say AI has been one of the most talked-about subjects on the app this year; this column asks how AI allegations against books and authors get handled on TikTok, and how well publishers and agencies respond to them.

Tom West, CEO of Publishers' Licensing Services, argues the AI-and-copyright argument is turning into an actual market: it is 'time for ideas to become solutions' in protecting authors' rights, with transparency the missing ingredient for a working licensing trade.

The Scholarly Kitchen's 'Chefs' weigh in on AI and copyright licensing: who should be paid for training data, what collective licensing could look like for publishers, and whether opt-out regimes are workable.
The Flowtica Verso is an always-on E Ink panel that clips to a phone, giving AI voice-recording and reading tools a screen instead of the usual screenless recorder form factor.

An essayist writing a book called 'Against Convenience' catalogues the tools she did and didn't allow herself — spell-check yes, chatbot no — and what the line between convenience and authorship actually is for a working writer.
The Guardian's books desk builds a reading list for making sense of the AI 'doom loop' — the titles that explain how the technology works, who profits, and what it is doing to writing and the web.

AI-generated 'slop' books are flooding online marketplaces, crowding listings and search results — and, insiders warn, squeezing the paychecks of human authors who now compete with machine-made titles for discovery.

A writer says he lost a $2m book deal after readers and detection tools mistook his African dialect prose for AI-generated text — a case study in how AI-detection culture is reshaping who gets published.

Calibre v9.15, the open-source ebook manager, ships an AI-powered 'Create Your Own Adventure' interactive fiction feature — putting a generative storytelling tool inside the library app millions of readers use to manage their books.

A new survey of writers shows a deep split on generative AI: a sizeable group now uses it for drafting, editing and marketing while another refuses on ethical grounds, with self-published authors adopting far faster than trade-published ones.
Booker winner Richard Flanagan attacks Australia's proposed text-and-data-mining exception, arguing the government is handing writers' work to 'AI colonists' and gutting the economics of authorship.
CharaLab has launched an AI manga generator that produces one- to six-panel comics in multiple art styles, aimed at creators and publishers who want to prototype comics pages faster.

Key findings from a blinded survey of 1,000 listeners comparing AI and human audiobook narration — how often listeners can tell the difference, and what it takes for synthetic narration to be accepted.

Illustrators in Malaysia — including book and cover artists — describe being hired to draw and then told to prompt instead, as studios and publishers fold generative tools into commissioned creative work.

A reading of 'Gulliver's Travels' 300 years on: Swift's writing machine on Laputa anticipated the AI text engine, and the essay argues it is an unsettling warning as AI floods classrooms, journals and publishing.
With AI drafts arriving in the slush pile, editors say the job has shifted: they now have to read the writer as well as the text, judging intent and provenance alongside prose.

AI detectors assume machine writing has predictable patterns — but so does careful human writing. A column on why writers are being pressured to abandon the em dash and other craft habits to prove they are human.
